6

Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can flag gen-2+ text for manual review
while retaining gen-1 content that preserves much
of the source distribution’s properties. Threeclass granularity is well-suited to this use case:
it separates human text from moderate-drift firstgeneration content and from deeper text with
compounding distributional shift—the distinction
most relevant to curation decisions. Finer-grained
depth distinctions may be achievable for nonparaphrastic chains (unlike paraphrastic chains,
which converge within ∼3 steps (Mohamed et al.,
2025)), but the three-class scheme already captures the practically relevant boundaries. The
tight cross-generator consistency of the ensemble
(CI width 1.4 pp) makes deployment feasible even
when the generating model is unknown.

Information value of the negative finding.
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (§4.4). This negative result carries positive information value: it
rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building
depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield
quality gains. The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition—consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication (Alemohammad et al., 2023).

Conclusion

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer
granularity. Across six generators from three
model families (0.6B–8.2B parameters), we documented differential depth response: centraltendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional
shape features remain near-stationary. A 7-feature
ensemble combining both feature types achieves
leave-one-generator-out macro-F1 of 0.79, with
per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to
0.86. We also reported that depth-aware data
curation does not improve downstream language
model quality over random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather
than curative tool.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0 / gen-1 / gen2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix C) yields
LOGO F1 ≈ 0.50, with depths 2–4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the
practical resolution limit.

710

Ethics Statement

711

726

All texts analyzed in this work are LLM-generated
from publicly available Wikipedia seeds; no
personal or sensitive data is involved.
Our
method estimates the generation depth of a text
passage—how many recursive generation steps it
has undergone—not the identity of its author. Individual authorship attribution is outside both the
scope and the capability of this approach; privacy implications are minimal. We acknowledge
that depth estimation tools could in principle be
used to selectively suppress machine-generated
text in contexts where such content is legitimate
(e.g., accessibility tools, assistive writing). We encourage deployment in data governance pipelines
where provenance transparency—rather than content removal—is the objective.

```text
1	To assess whether depth signal extends beyond handcrafted features, we fine-tune a pretrained language model end-to-end as a depth classifier using QLoRA \cite{qlora}.
2	
3	\paragraph{Setup.}
4	We fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B-Base with LoRA rank 16, learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$, and 3 epochs on the same 6-generator dataset used throughout, framing depth estimation as 5-class sequence classification (gen-0 through gen-4).
5	For 3-class evaluation, we collapse predictions into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ post hoc.
6	All results use the same LOGO protocol as the main experiments.
7	
8	\begin{table}[h]
9	\centering
10	\small
11	\caption{QLoRA end-to-end depth classification vs.\ XGBoost on handcrafted features, under LOGO evaluation.}
12	\label{tab:qlora}
13	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
14	\toprule
15	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{5-class F1} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Per-class F1 (5-class)} \\
16	\midrule
17	XGBoost (7 features) & 0.501 $\pm$ 0.038 & 0.789 & --- \\
18	QLoRA (Qwen3-0.6B)   & 0.583 $\pm$ 0.010 & 0.905 $\pm$ 0.003 & 0.999\,/\,0.796\,/\,0.413\,/\,0.259\,/\,0.447 \\
19	\bottomrule
20	\end{tabular}
21	\end{table}
22	
23	\paragraph{Results.}
24	QLoRA achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.003), a +11.6\,pp improvement over the XGBoost baseline (0.789).
25	On 5-class evaluation, QLoRA reaches F1\,=\,0.583 ($\pm$0.010) vs.\ 0.501 for XGBoost (+8.2\,pp), with the largest gains at gen-1 (0.796 vs.\ 0.634) and gen-2 (0.413 vs.\ 0.268).
26	The gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains the primary failure mode (gen-3 F1\,=\,0.259), consistent with the feature-level analysis in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
27	
28	\paragraph{Hyperparameter robustness.}
29	A second run with LoRA rank 32 and seed 123 yields 5-class F1\,=\,0.587 ($\pm$0.005) and 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.004), confirming stability across hyperparameter and seed variation ($\Delta < 1$\,pp on both metrics).
30	
31	\paragraph{Implications.}
32	The substantial 3-class improvement demonstrates that raw token embeddings contain depth signal beyond what summary statistics capture---the seven handcrafted features are a strong but lossy compression of the full distributional information.
33	End-to-end fine-tuning exploits token-level patterns (e.g., positional regularities, n-gram repetitions) that aggregate features cannot represent.
34	This confirms that the depth signal documented in our main analysis is real and exploitable beyond engineered features, while the handcrafted approach retains practical advantages: interpretability, computational efficiency (no GPU inference), and the ability to reveal the differential depth response pattern that motivates the task formulation.
35	
```

Based on the search results, here's what I found about SemEval 2024 Task 8's Subtasks B and C:

## Subtask B: Multi-class Machine-Generated Text Detection

Subtask B is to detect the exact source of a text, discerning whether it is written by a human or generated by a specific LLM. More specifically, given a full text, the task is to determine who generated it, as it can be human-written or generated by a specific language model.

Subtask B deals with multi-class classification task. The subtask attracted 70 participants.

## Subtask C: Human-Machine Mixed Text Detection

Subtask C aims to identify the changing point within a text, at which the authorship transitions from human to machine. More specifically, given a mixed text, where the first part is human-written and the second part is machine-generated, the task is to determine the boundary, where the change occurs.

Subtask C attracted 30 participants. Subtasks A and B were relatively easier, with all systems showing improvements over the baseline. However, Subtask C proved to be significantly more challenging.

## Overall Results

For all subtasks, the best systems used LLMs.

Based on the search results, I found relevant research on AI-generated text detection with multi-class classification from 2025, as well as information about recursive generation and synthetic text detection. Here are the key findings:

## AI-Generated Text Detection with Multi-Class Classification (2025)

A research paper addressed two sub-tasks at AAAI 2025 under the AI-Generated Text Detection shared task: Task A involved distinguishing between human-authored or AI-generated text, while Task B focused on attributing text to its originating language model. The optimized architecture secured fifth place with an F1 score of 0.994 for the binary classification task, while the simple architecture achieved fifth place with an F1 score of 0.627 for the multiclass classification task.

## Synthetic Text Detection Approaches

A novel approach for multilingual AI-generated text detection uses self-supervised learning, enabling models to deeply learn structural and semantic features of a language, followed by supervised fine-tuning to customize the model's capability for detecting synthetic text.

## Recursive Paraphrasing and Detection Evasion

Research has shown that recursive paraphrase can significantly reduce detection rates for AI-generated text. A framework called TempParaphraser segments text into individual sentences and then paraphrases each sentence multiple times.

## Recursive Generation and Model Collapse

AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data, according to research published in Nature 2024.

The search results show active research in 2025 on detecting AI-generated text across multiple classification tasks, with particular attention to robustness challenges posed by recursive paraphrasing and synthetic data generation.

## LLM-Generated Text Detection Research

LLM-generated text detection is conceptualized as a binary classification task that seeks to determine whether an LLM produced a given text. Recent advances in this field stem from innovations in watermarking techniques, statistics-based detectors, and neural-based detectors.

## Generation Chains and Reasoning Approaches

Your query mentions "generation chains," which relates to recent developments in LLM reasoning. Encouraging LLMs to produce more intermediate steps through a Chain of Thought can enhance their effectiveness. ## Detection Benchmarks and Real-World Challenges

DetectRL is a new benchmark that includes popular LLMs, abuse-prone domains, well-designed attacks, and varying text lengths. However, the reliability of existing detectors in real-world applications remains underexplored, with state-of-the-art detection techniques still underperforming in this task.

## Recent 2026 Detection Advances

Text generated by large language models, especially reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1, usually exhibits higher SeqProbScore values because their generation strategies (e.g., chain-of-thought) tend to consistently follow high-probability token paths.

I've completed the web search on iterative generation, recursive rewriting, LLM text quality degradation detection, and related research from 2025-2026. Here are the key findings:

## Recursive Language Models and Iterative Processing

Research explores language models that recursively call themselves or other LLMs to mitigate degradation "context rot". Context rot is a phenomenon where model performance degrades as a function of context length.

Recursive Language Models (RLMs) successfully handle inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows and dramatically outperform the quality of base LLMs across diverse long-context tasks.

## Information Distortion Through Iterative Generation

A significant 2025 study addresses quality degradation detection: Research investigates whether LLMs distort information through iterative generation like a "broken telephone" effect, finding that distortion accumulates over time, influenced by language choice and chain complexity.

Current evaluations are generally confined to single iterations and fail to capture the cumulative degradation introduced by iterative generation, with recent work addressing this gap by providing rigorous analysis of deterioration across successive iterations in both translation and rephrasing tasks.

## Detection and Mitigation

While degradation is inevitable, it can be mitigated through strategic prompting techniques.

Counterexample-guided iterative refinement, logic- and sample-based semantic checks, or classifier-based semantic similarity constraints are employed to address hallucinations or errors in LLM-generated rewrites.

The research indicates this is an active area of investigation with both practical solutions for long-context processing and methods for detecting and mitigating quality degradation in iterative LLM workflows.

Context rot is a phenomenon where model performance degrades as a function of context length.\n\nRecursive Language Models (RLMs) successfully handle inputs up to two orders of magnitude beyond model context windows and dramatically outperform the quality of base LLMs across diverse long-context tasks.\n\n## Information Distortion Through Iterative Generation\n\nA significant 2025 study addresses quality degradation detection: Research investigates whether LLMs distort information through iterative generation like a \"broken telephone\" effect, finding that distortion accumulates over time, influenced by language choice and chain complexity.\n\nCurrent evaluations are generally confined to single iterations and fail to capture the cumulative degradation introduced by iterative generation, with recent work addressing this gap by providing rigorous analysis of deterioration across successive iterations in both translation and rephrasing tasks.\n\n## Detection and Mitigation\n\nWhile degradation is inevitable, it can be mitigated through strategic prompting techniques.\n\nCounterexample-guided iterative refinement, logic- and sample-based semantic checks, or classifier-based semantic similarity constraints are employed to address hallucinations or errors in LLM-generated rewrites.\n\nThe research indicates this is an active area of investigation with both practical solutions for long-context processing and methods for detecting and mitigating quality degradation in iterative LLM workflows."

```text
1	% Appendix A — Length Confound Analysis
2	% Data source: plan-013 (23,032 samples, 5 generators)
3	
4	Surface diversity features (TTR, hapax ratio) mechanically depend on text length:
5	shorter texts yield higher type-token ratios by construction.
6	If generation depth systematically shortens text, observed depth trends could be length artifacts rather than genuine distributional shifts.
7	We rule this out with three complementary analyses.
8	
9	\paragraph{(a) Length--depth correlation.}
10	We compute Spearman rank correlation between word count and depth across all five generators.
11	Correlations are weak and inconsistent in sign:
12	$\rho$ ranges from $-0.066$ (Pythia-1B) to $+0.134$ (OLMo-2-1B), with $|\rho| < 0.14$ in every case.
13	One generator (Qwen3-0.6B) shows no significant correlation ($\rho = 0.012$, $p = 0.43$).
14	Length and depth are thus near-independent in our corpus.
15	
16	\paragraph{(b) Length-normalized feature trends.}
17	To eliminate residual length effects, we recompute TTR and hapax ratio on fixed 200-word windows.
18	After normalization, monotonic depth trends are fully preserved for all generators; moreover, Spearman correlations between normalized features and depth \emph{increase} in absolute value (e.g., Pythia-2.8B TTR: $\rho = -0.633 \to -0.715$).
19	Length removal sharpens the depth signal rather than diminishing it, confirming that the signal is not a length artifact.
20	
21	\paragraph{(c) Length-matched classification.}
22	We subsample the dataset so that word-count distributions are equalized across depth classes, then retrain the 3-class XGBoost classifier (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}).
23	Macro-F1 changes by $\Delta = +0.041$ relative to the unmatched baseline---performance \emph{improves} when length variance is removed.
24	This is consistent with length acting as noise rather than signal.
25	
26	\paragraph{Conclusion.}
27	We observe a dropout bias: shorter texts are more likely to fall below the minimum-length threshold at deeper generation stages.
28	However, this bias does not drive the depth fingerprint.
29	All three analyses converge on the same conclusion: the depth signal captured by our feature ensemble is independent of text-length variation.
30	
```
